analysis.one_liner: Wipes out EPA limits on greenhouse gas pollution from coal- and gas-fired power plants.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would strike down the EPA's 2024 limits on greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel power plants, was referred to committee in February 2025 and got no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill declares that a May 2024 EPA rule has no force or effect. That rule set the first national limits on greenhouse gas emissions from coal-fired power plants and standards for new and modified gas-fired plants, generally requiring plants to cut emissions sharply or capture carbon. The bill would erase those requirements, leaving no federal limit on power plant carbon pollution.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of coal-fired power plants and the coal mining industry, which would avoid the cost of retrofitting plants with carbon capture or retiring them on the rule's timeline. Utility companies would also avoid compliance costs that could otherwise be passed to ratepayers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal plant owners and coal mining

how_it_helps.text: The bill's single provision states that the 2024 EPA power plant rule "shall have no force or effect," removing every requirement in it. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: People living near power plants, who would continue to breathe the particulate matter and other pollutants that come with burning coal and gas without limits tied to the rule, and the public generally, which bears the costs of unchecked greenhouse gas emissions. Future ratepayers could face higher costs if deferred investments in cleaner generation come due later.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near power plants and the public

drawbacks.text: Nullifying the rule leaves greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel-fired power plants unregulated at the federal level, which is the source of the public health and climate costs avoided only by keeping the rule in force. [S2]
Supporters of the rule argue the compliance costs are the price of limiting pollution; the bill takes the cost side without addressing the emissions the rule was written to control. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is concentrated and immediate: coal plant owners and the coal industry avoid retrofit or closure costs, and electricity prices may rise less than under the rule. The cost is diffuse and long-term: no federal limit on power plant carbon pollution, and continued local air pollution for plant communities. The bill repeals the rule entirely rather than modifying or delaying it, so it offers no alternative path for reducing those emissions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which took no action on it, so it never came to a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Troy Balderson introduced the bill on February 27, 2025, with 11 original cosponsors. [S2]
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day. [S4]
The bill attracted 37 cosponsors, all Republicans, and no further action was taken after the referral. [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The EPA's power plant rule remains in force for now, so communities near power plants and the public retain the emissions limits the bill would have erased. Nothing in the record shows the bill received committee consideration, so no one had to vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities near power plants, for now

for.name: Troy Balderson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to nullify the EPA power plant rule.

for.name: 37 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of the 37 cosponsors is a Democrat.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no markup or committee vote was scheduled, and no floor vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: All 37 cosponsors are Republicans and no Democrat signed on; the bill drew no Democratic support and never reached a vote.

industries.note: The 2024 rule would require existing coal plants to cut their greenhouse gas emissions on a set schedule, which for many plants means costly carbon capture equipment or closure. Nullifying the rule spares owners those costs by leaving their emissions unregulated, with the pollution burden falling on nearby communities and the public.
Emissions limits that push coal plants toward capture or retirement reduce demand for coal. The bill removes that pressure, preserving coal's market in electricity generation.
The rule sets standards for new and modified gas-fired generating units; nullifying it removes those requirements for future gas plant construction.

Utilities avoid compliance costs, which supporters argue protects ratepayers from price increases, but they also lose regulatory certainty and would face the emissions consequences of plants they continue to operate without limits.

industries.industry: Carbon capture and clean energy suppliers
industries.note: The rule creates demand for carbon capture retrofits and replacement generation; erasing it removes that market signal.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action more than a year after referral, the bill is unlikely to reach the floor this Congress and would typically die when it ends in January 2027. Separately, the EPA could revisit or rescind the rule through its own rulemaking, which would accomplish much of what this bill seeks without Congress.
